title: Energy and Thermodynamics
bigQuestion: If energy can never be created or destroyed, why do we keep running out of it?

story.title: The Brewer's Son Who Weighed Heat
story.kicker: In a Manchester cellar, a young man let weights fall over and over to answer one question: what is heat made of?
paragraphs: In the 1840s most scientists believed heat was a fluid. They called it caloric, an invisible, weightless substance that flowed from hot things into cold ones. James Prescott Joule did not believe it. Joule was the son of a brewer in Salford, next to Manchester, England. He had no university post. What he had was a home laboratory, a brewer's habit of measuring temperature very precisely, and a stubborn idea: heat was not a substance at all. It was motion, and you could make it with ordinary mechanical work.

His apparatus looked almost like a toy. A brass paddle wheel sat inside a copper can full of water. Strings ran from the wheel over pulleys to two heavy weights. When the weights fell, the strings spun the paddles and churned the water. Fixed vanes inside the can kept the water from simply spinning along, so the paddles had to fight through it. Joule knew exactly how far the weights fell and how heavy they were, so he knew exactly how much work gravity had done. Then he read the water's temperature with a thermometer he could trust to a small fraction of a degree.

The rise was tiny. After twenty falls of the weights, the water was warmer by well under one degree Fahrenheit. Joule spent hours on each run, waiting for the water to settle, and corrected for the warmth of his own body and the room. He repeated it with mercury instead of water and with iron plates rubbing together instead of paddles. Every time, the same amount of work made the same amount of heat. In 1845 he told a scientific meeting in Cambridge; the story goes that the chairman asked him to keep it short, and almost nobody cared.

One listener did. A young William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, thought Joule might be right, and the two became allies. In 1850 Joule published his full results: raising one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit took the work of a 772-pound weight falling one foot. In today's units that is about 4.2 joules for every calorie, within roughly one percent of the modern value. Heat was energy. It could be made from work, and work could be made from it. The unit of energy now carries his name.
story.think: Joule's temperature changes were fractions of a degree. Why might a tiny, carefully repeated effect be more convincing than a large, sloppy one?

lessons.title: What Counts as Work
lessons.mainIdea: In physics, work is done only when a force moves something along the direction of the force.
reading: Hold a heavy backpack at arm's length for one minute. Your arm burns, but by the physics definition you have done no *work* on the backpack. Work needs two things: a force, and movement along the direction of that force. The backpack did not move, so the work is zero. Your muscles get tired because they keep twitching and burning fuel to hold the force, but none of that energy went into the backpack.

Now lift the backpack one meter straight up. You push up with a force about equal to its weight, and it moves up one meter. Work equals force times distance, written W = F d. A 10-newton backpack lifted 1 meter takes 10 newton-meters of work. Physicists call one newton-meter a *joule*, after the man in the story. A joule is small: lifting an apple from the table to your mouth takes roughly one joule.

Direction matters. If you carry the backpack across a flat floor at steady speed, the upward force from your arm is at right angles to the sideways motion, so it does no work at all. When a force pushes at an angle, only the part along the motion counts. A force that points against the motion, like friction on a sliding box, does negative work: it takes energy out of the box's motion and turns it into heat.

This narrow definition is what makes energy a useful idea. Because work is defined so precisely, we can add it up, track where it goes, and always find the total. That bookkeeping is the whole story of this chapter.

words.d: force times the distance moved in the direction of the force, measured in joules
the unit of energy and work; one newton of force acting through one meter
the unit of force; a small apple weighs about one newton on Earth

look.title: Three Ways to Move a Box
look.text: A mover slides a 200-newton box 3 meters across a rough floor, pushing with 80 newtons. Then she lifts the same box 1 meter onto a truck bed. Finally she carries it 10 meters along the flat truck bed at steady speed.
look.prompt: Rank the three jobs by the work done on the box, and explain why carrying it along the bed is the odd one out.

check.q: A student holds a 50-newton weight motionless above her head for 30 seconds. How much work does she do on the weight?
choices: Zero, because the weight does not move
It cannot be known without the height
check.why: Work needs motion along the force. The weight does not move, so the work on it is zero, even though her muscles tire.

check.q: Lifting a 20-newton bag 2 meters straight up takes how much work?
check.why: Work is force times distance: 20 newtons times 2 meters equals 40 joules.

check.q: Friction acts on a sled sliding across ice. What is the sign of the work friction does on the sled?
choices: Positive, because friction is a force
Negative, because friction points against the motion
Positive, because the sled heats up
check.why: Friction points opposite to the motion, so it removes energy from the sled's motion. That is negative work.

lessons.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Energy of motion depends on mass and the square of speed; stored gravitational energy depends on mass, gravity and height.
reading: A bowling ball rolling down a lane can knock over pins. It carries *kinetic energy*, the energy of motion. The formula is KE = 1/2 m v squared, where m is mass in kilograms and v is speed in meters per second. The square is the important part. Double a car's speed and its kinetic energy is four times larger. That is why highway crashes are so much worse than parking-lot bumps: stopping the car means removing all of that energy, and it has to go somewhere, usually into crumpled metal.

Now imagine the bowling ball resting on a shelf two meters up. It is not moving, but it could. Push it off and gravity will speed it up. We say it holds *gravitational potential energy*, energy stored by position. The formula is PE = m g h, where g is the strength of gravity, about 9.8 newtons per kilogram near Earth's surface, and h is the height. Lifting the ball to the shelf took work, and that work is now banked in the ball's height.

The two forms trade back and forth. As the ball falls, its height shrinks and its speed grows. Potential energy becomes kinetic energy, joule for joule. A 7-kilogram ball on a 2-meter shelf holds about 137 joules of potential energy. Just before it hits the floor, if air resistance is small, it has about 137 joules of kinetic energy, which works out to a speed of roughly 6.3 meters per second.

Height is always measured from somewhere, and you get to choose where. Potential energy on a shelf is 137 joules relative to the floor, but zero relative to the shelf itself. Only changes in potential energy matter, so pick the reference that makes the problem easiest.

words.d: the energy an object has because it is moving; half its mass times its speed squared
energy stored by an object's height above a chosen reference level
the height you choose to call zero when calculating potential energy

look.title: Two Cars, One Wall
look.text: Two identical cars head toward a test wall. One travels at 30 kilometers per hour and the other at 60 kilometers per hour. Engineers measure how much the front end crumples. The faster car's crumple zone is crushed far more than twice as badly.
look.prompt: Use the kinetic energy formula to explain why doubling the speed does not merely double the damage.

check.q: A cart's speed triples. Its kinetic energy becomes:
check.why: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Three squared is nine, so the energy is nine times larger.

check.q: Which change stores the most extra gravitational potential energy?
check.why: Potential energy is m g h. The products are 6, 4, 5 and 4.5 kilogram-meters, so 2 kilograms times 3 meters stores the most.

check.q: A ball is dropped from a shelf. Ignoring air resistance, what happens to its total mechanical energy as it falls?
choices: It grows because the ball speeds up
It stays the same while potential energy turns into kinetic energy
It shrinks because the ball loses height
It becomes zero at the halfway point
check.why: Height is traded for speed. The sum of potential and kinetic energy stays constant if nothing else, like air drag, is acting.

lessons.title: Power Is Energy per Second
lessons.mainIdea: Power measures how fast energy is transferred, in joules per second, called watts.
reading: Two students carry identical boxes up the same stairs. One takes ten seconds, the other takes a full minute. They do the same work, because the force and the height are the same. But the first student is more powerful. *Power* is the rate of doing work, energy divided by time. Its unit is the *watt*, one joule per second, named for James Watt, the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine in the 1770s.

Watts show up on almost everything you plug in. A phone charger might draw 20 watts, a hair dryer 1500 watts, a microwave oven about 1000 watts. That means the microwave turns about 1000 joules of electrical energy into heat and microwaves every second. A resting human body runs at roughly 100 watts, most of it leaving as heat, which is why a crowded room warms up.

Your electric bill is not in watts but in *kilowatt-hours*. A kilowatt-hour is one thousand watts running for one hour, which equals 3.6 million joules. It is an energy unit, not a power unit, even though it has the word watt inside it. Running a 1000-watt microwave for six minutes uses one tenth of a kilowatt-hour. Illinois households pay a price per kilowatt-hour, so the cost of a device depends on both its wattage and how long it runs.

Power also explains why a car needs a big engine to climb a hill fast but a small one to climb it slowly. The work of lifting the car is fixed by its weight and the hill's height. Doing that work in less time takes more power, and an engine's power is what limits its speed uphill.

words.d: the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred; energy divided by time
the unit of power; one joule per second
an energy unit equal to 1000 watts for one hour, or 3.6 million joules

look.title: Typical Power of Everyday Things
rows: Small car engine at full output
look.prompt: About how many resting people would it take to match the energy output of one hair dryer, and why does that comparison feel surprising?

check.q: A motor does 600 joules of work in 20 seconds. What is its power?
check.why: Power is work divided by time: 600 joules divided by 20 seconds is 30 watts.

check.q: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of:
check.why: A kilowatt-hour is power multiplied by time, which gives energy. It equals 3.6 million joules.

check.q: Two elevators lift the same load to the same floor. Elevator A takes 8 seconds and elevator B takes 16 seconds. Which is true?
choices: A uses twice the power but does the same work
check.why: The work is identical because force and height are the same. A does it in half the time, so its power is twice as large.

lessons.title: Energy Is Never Lost, Only Moved
lessons.mainIdea: In a closed system the total energy stays constant; energy bar charts let you track where it goes.
reading: Drop a rubber ball and it bounces, but each bounce is lower than the last. Where did the energy go? Not nowhere. Each time the ball squashes against the floor, some of its energy turns into a bit of heat in the rubber and a bit of sound in the air. The ball's mechanical energy shrinks, but the total energy of ball, floor and air does not change. This is the *law of conservation of energy*: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another or moved from one object to another.

The cleanest way to see it is an *energy bar chart*. Draw a bar for each form of energy at the start: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal. Draw the same bars at the end. If the system is closed, the total height of all the bars is the same in both pictures. A roller coaster at the top of its first hill has a tall potential bar and a tiny kinetic bar. At the bottom, the bars have swapped, and a small thermal bar has grown from friction on the rails.

The word system is the key. If you decide the system is just the ball, then the floor and air are outside it, and energy leaves the system as heat and sound. If you decide the system is ball, floor and air together, nothing leaves. Both are correct. The law says only that whatever crosses the boundary must be counted as work or heat flowing in or out.
Engineers use this bookkeeping every day. Energy that leaks out as heat is usually wasted, so tracking where each joule goes tells you where to make a machine better.

words.d: the total energy of a closed system stays the same; energy changes form but is never created or destroyed
a diagram with one bar for each form of energy, drawn before and after an event to track the total
a chosen set of objects that no energy enters or leaves
the energy of the random jiggling of atoms and molecules in a material

look.title: The Pendulum and the Nose
look.text: A physics teacher hangs a heavy bowling ball from the ceiling on a rope. She pulls it back until it touches her nose, holds it still, and lets go without pushing. The ball swings across the room and back toward her face. She does not flinch, and the ball stops a hair short of her nose.
look.prompt: Explain, using conservation of energy, why the ball cannot come back higher than where it started, and what would happen if she gave it a small push.

check.q: A bouncing ball rises less with each bounce. Which statement is correct?
choices: Energy was destroyed on each bounce
The ball's mechanical energy became thermal energy and sound
Gravity got stronger with each bounce
The ball lost mass on each bounce
check.why: Energy is conserved. The ball's motion energy turned into heat in the rubber and floor and into sound, so less was left for height.

check.q: On an energy bar chart for a closed system, what must be true of the before and after pictures?
choices: The kinetic bar is always taller after
The thermal bar is always zero
The total height of all bars is the same
Each bar keeps its own height
check.why: Individual forms of energy change, but in a closed system their sum does not. The total bar height stays constant.

check.q: A skier starts from rest at the top of a hill. At the bottom she is slower than the frictionless prediction. The missing energy is:
choices: thermal energy in the snow and skis
check.why: Friction between skis and snow does negative work on the skier, turning some of her kinetic energy into heat.

lessons.title: Springs and Stored Energy
lessons.mainIdea: A spring's force grows in proportion to how far it is stretched, and the energy it stores grows with the square of that stretch.
reading: Pull a spring a little and it pulls back a little. Pull it twice as far and it pulls back twice as hard. Robert Hooke described this in the 1670s, and it is now called *Hooke's law*: the restoring force equals a constant times the stretch, F = k x. The constant k is the *spring constant*, measured in newtons per meter. A stiff car suspension spring might have k in the tens of thousands of newtons per meter; a slinky's is far smaller.

Because the force grows as you stretch, the work to stretch a spring is not simply force times distance. The average force during the stretch is half the final force, so the stored *elastic potential energy* is PE = 1/2 k x squared. Like kinetic energy, it has a square in it. Stretch a spring twice as far and you store four times the energy. That is why a fully drawn bow launches an arrow so much faster than a half-drawn one.

Hooke's law only holds up to a point. Stretch a spring too far and it stops springing back; it has passed its elastic limit and is permanently bent. Many materials obey the law for small stretches, which is why a diving board, a guitar string, a trampoline and even a steel bridge girder all behave a bit like springs. Engineers measure k for each and design so that loads stay well within the elastic range.

Rubber bands look like springs but are not perfect ones. Their force does not grow in a straight line with stretch, and they warm up noticeably when stretched and released quickly, a sign that some of the work becomes heat instead of stored energy.

words.d: the force from a spring is proportional to how far it is stretched or squeezed: F = k x
the stiffness of a spring, k, in newtons per meter of stretch
energy stored in a stretched or squeezed object; half k times the stretch squared
the stretch beyond which a material no longer springs back to its original shape

look.title: A Spring Under Load
look.cite: example classroom data for a light spring
look.prompt: What is the spring constant in newtons per centimeter, and how much energy is stored at 5 newtons compared with 2.5 newtons?

check.q: A spring with k = 200 newtons per meter is stretched 0.1 meter. How much force does it pull back with?
check.why: Hooke's law: F = k x = 200 times 0.1 = 20 newtons.

check.q: If you stretch a spring three times as far, the stored elastic energy is:
check.why: Elastic energy is half k x squared, so tripling x multiplies the energy by nine.

check.q: A spring is stretched past its elastic limit. Which best describes what happens?
choices: It stays bent and no longer returns to its original length
check.why: Beyond the elastic limit, the material deforms permanently and Hooke's law no longer applies.

lessons.title: Back and Forth: Oscillation
lessons.mainIdea: A mass on a spring or a pendulum swings back and forth because a restoring force keeps trading potential energy for kinetic energy.
reading: Pull a mass hanging from a spring down a few centimeters and let go. It rises, overshoots, falls back, overshoots again, and keeps going. This repeating motion is *oscillation*. Energy sloshes between elastic potential energy at the ends of the swing, where the mass momentarily stops, and kinetic energy in the middle, where it moves fastest. Nothing pushes it after the first tug; the spring's own restoring force does all the work.

The time for one full back-and-forth is the *period*. For a mass on a spring, a heavier mass makes the period longer and a stiffer spring makes it shorter. For a *pendulum*, something surprising happens: the period depends on the length of the string and the strength of gravity, but not on the mass of the bob, and for small swings not on how wide the swing is. Galileo is said to have noticed this watching a lamp swing in a cathedral. A pendulum about one meter long takes almost exactly two seconds for a full swing on Earth.

That steady period is why pendulums ran clocks for three hundred years. A grandfather clock's pendulum ticks once per second in each direction. Friction and air drag slowly steal energy, so the swings shrink; a weight or spring inside the clock gives a tiny push each swing to make up the loss. Without that push the oscillation is *damped* and eventually stops.

The site's drum bench and wave bench are oscillators too. A drumhead struck in the middle springs up and down hundreds of times a second, and that rate sets the pitch. The same physics that swings a pendulum also makes a bridge sway in wind and an atom vibrate in a crystal.

words.d: motion that repeats back and forth around a rest position
the time for one complete back-and-forth cycle
a mass hanging from a string or rod that swings under gravity
describes an oscillation whose swings shrink over time because energy is lost to friction or drag

look.title: Two Pendulums, Two Bobs
look.text: A student hangs a steel ball and a wooden ball of the same size from strings of the same length. She pulls both back the same small distance and releases them at the same moment. She expects the heavy steel ball to swing faster.
look.prompt: Predict what she actually sees, and explain it using the fact that gravity accelerates all masses equally.

check.q: Where in its swing does a pendulum bob have the most kinetic energy?
choices: At the bottom of the swing, where it moves fastest
At the highest point on the left
At the highest point on the right
Kinetic energy is the same everywhere
check.why: At the bottom the bob has traded all its extra height for speed, so kinetic energy is greatest there.

check.q: Which change makes a pendulum's period longer?
choices: Pulling it back a tiny bit less
Painting the bob a darker color
check.why: For small swings the period depends only on string length and gravity. A longer string means a longer period.

check.q: A mass on a spring bounces with smaller and smaller swings and finally stops. This is because:
choices: friction and drag turned the motion energy into heat
check.why: The oscillation is damped. Each cycle, a little mechanical energy becomes thermal energy, until none is left.

lessons.title: Temperature Is Not Heat
lessons.mainIdea: Temperature measures the average energy of jiggling molecules; heat is energy flowing from a hotter object to a colder one.
reading: A bathtub of warm water and a single spark from a sparkler: which is hotter? The spark, by far, at well over a thousand degrees. Which holds more thermal energy? The bathtub, by an enormous margin. That is the difference between *temperature* and thermal energy. Temperature measures how hard, on average, each molecule is jiggling. Thermal energy is the total for all the molecules put together. The spark has few molecules moving very fast; the tub has trillions of trillions moving gently.

*Heat* is a third idea, and the word is used carelessly in everyday speech. In physics, heat is energy in transit, moving from a hotter object to a colder one because of the temperature difference. A hot pan does not contain heat; it contains thermal energy. When you touch it, heat flows into your hand. Once the energy arrives it is thermal energy again. Joule's paddle wheel showed that this flowing energy is the same stuff as work, measured in the same joules.

Heat moves three ways. *Conduction* is molecule bumping molecule, the way a metal spoon in soup grows hot at the handle. *Convection* is hot fluid physically moving, the way warm air rises off a radiator. Radiation is light, including infrared light you cannot see, the way the Sun warms your face across empty space. On a Chicago January morning all three are pulling heat out of you: the cold air by conduction, the wind by convection, and the dark sky by radiation.

Temperature has a floor. Cool a gas and its molecules slow down; at about minus 273 degrees Celsius they would have the least energy physically possible. That is *absolute zero*, the zero of the Kelvin scale. Nothing has ever reached it, though laboratories have come within billionths of a degree.

words.d: a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance
energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder one because of the temperature difference
heat transfer by particles bumping into their neighbors, mostly in solids
heat transfer by the movement of a heated liquid or gas
the lowest possible temperature, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, or 0 kelvin

look.title: Metal and Wood on a Winter Porch
look.text: A metal railing and a wooden rail sit side by side on a porch in Rockford in January. A thermometer shows both are at the same temperature, minus 10 degrees Celsius. A student touches each with a bare hand. The metal feels painfully colder than the wood.
look.prompt: If both are at the same temperature, what is different about the two materials that makes the metal feel colder? Which of the three kinds of heat transfer is involved?

check.q: A cup of coffee at 80 degrees Celsius and a swimming pool at 25 degrees Celsius. Which statement is true?
choices: The coffee has more thermal energy
The pool has more thermal energy
They have the same thermal energy
Temperature and thermal energy are the same thing
check.why: The coffee is hotter, but the pool has vastly more molecules, so its total thermal energy is far larger.

check.q: In physics, heat is best described as:
choices: a fluid that hot objects contain
energy moving from hot to cold because of a temperature difference
the speed of the fastest molecule
check.why: Heat is energy in transit driven by a temperature difference. Joule showed it is not a substance.

check.q: A warm current of air rises from a heater and spreads across a room. This is mainly:
check.why: Convection is heat carried by the bulk movement of a fluid, here the rising warm air.

lessons.title: Specific Heat and Lake Michigan
lessons.mainIdea: Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm by one degree, and water needs far more than most.
reading: On a hot August afternoon the sand at a Lake Michigan beach can burn your feet while the water is still cool. Sand and water sit under the same sun, yet the sand heats up fast and the water hardly changes. The property behind this is *specific heat*: the energy needed to raise one kilogram of a material by one degree Celsius. Water's is about 4200 joules per kilogram per degree, among the highest of any common substance. Dry sand's is roughly 800, so the same sunlight warms sand about five times as much.

The formula is Q = m c delta T: heat added equals mass times specific heat times the temperature change. Heat 2 kilograms of water from 20 to 100 degrees and you need 2 times 4200 times 80, about 670,000 joules. That is why a kettle takes minutes even at 1500 watts. Heat the same mass of iron by the same amount and you need only about a ninth as much energy, because iron's specific heat is around 450.

Water's high specific heat shapes Chicago's weather. Lake Michigan warms slowly in spring and cools slowly in fall, so lakefront neighborhoods are cooler than the western suburbs in May and milder in November. Weather forecasters say cooler near the lake for exactly this reason. The oceans do the same on a planetary scale, soaking up enormous amounts of heat and smoothing the seasons for coastal regions.

Specific heat also explains Joule's choice of water. Because water takes so much energy to warm, his temperature rises were tiny and hard to read. But water is easy to measure and stir, and its specific heat was already the standard definition of the calorie, so his result could be compared with everyone else's.

words.d: the energy needed to raise one kilogram of a material by one degree Celsius
the energy that warms one gram of water by one degree Celsius; about 4.2 joules
the change in temperature, final minus starting

look.title: Specific Heat of Common Materials
look.unit: joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, rounded
look.prompt: Equal masses of water and lead each receive 1000 joules. Which warms more, and by roughly how many times?

check.q: How much energy warms 0.5 kilogram of water by 10 degrees Celsius? Use 4200 joules per kilogram per degree.
check.why: Q = m c delta T = 0.5 times 4200 times 10 = 21,000 joules.

check.q: Equal masses of copper and water sit in the same sunlight. After ten minutes the copper is much hotter. Why?
choices: Copper absorbs more sunlight per kilogram than anything else
Copper's specific heat is much lower, so each joule raises its temperature more
Copper has more molecules per kilogram
check.why: Specific heat of copper is about 385 versus 4200 for water. The same energy raises copper's temperature roughly eleven times more.

check.q: Why are Chicago lakefront neighborhoods cooler than inland suburbs on a hot May afternoon?
choices: The lake reflects the sunlight away
Lake water is always at 4 degrees Celsius
Water's high specific heat means the lake warms slowly and cools the air passing over it
The lake produces its own cold wind from evaporation only
check.why: Lake Michigan takes weeks to warm because of water's high specific heat, so air moving off the lake is cooler.

lessons.title: The Laws of Thermodynamics
lessons.mainIdea: The first law says energy is conserved when heat and work are both counted; the second says heat flows on its own only from hot to cold.
reading: Thermodynamics began as the science of steam engines and grew into rules that govern everything from stars to cells. The *first law of thermodynamics* is conservation of energy written for heat. The change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it minus the work it does on its surroundings. Pump air into a bicycle tire and the pump gets warm: you did work on the air, and its internal energy and temperature rose. Let compressed air rush out and it feels cold: the air did work pushing outward, and its internal energy fell.

The first law allows many things that never happen. Nothing in it forbids a cold cup of coffee from spontaneously pulling heat out of the room and becoming hot again. Energy would still be conserved. Yet it never occurs. The *second law of thermodynamics* explains why: heat flows on its own only from hotter to colder, never the reverse. Rudolf Clausius stated it this way in the 1850s. You can move heat from cold to hot, as a refrigerator does, but only by doing work, and the work always ends up as extra heat somewhere.

There is a *zeroth law*, named later because it turned out to be more basic. If two objects are each in thermal balance with a third, they are in balance with each other. That is what makes a thermometer work: it settles at the temperature of whatever it touches. And a *third law* says absolute zero can be approached but never reached in a finite number of steps.

These laws are not derived from anything deeper. They are summaries of what has been observed, without exception, in every experiment ever done. Patent offices refuse machines that would violate them, and no proposed perpetual-motion machine has ever run.

words.d: a system's internal energy changes by the heat added minus the work it does
heat never flows on its own from a colder object to a hotter one
the total energy stored inside a substance in the motion and arrangement of its particles
two objects each in thermal balance with a third are in balance with each other

look.title: Clausius Sums Up the Universe
look.text: In an 1865 paper, the German physicist Rudolf Clausius, who had introduced the word entropy, ended with two sentences, in translation: The energy of the universe is constant. The entropy of the universe tends toward a maximum.
look.cite: Rudolf Clausius, paper on the mechanical theory of heat, 1865 (translated from German)
look.prompt: Which of Clausius's two sentences states the first law and which states the second? Why did he choose the whole universe as his system?

check.q: A gas in a cylinder absorbs 500 joules of heat and does 200 joules of work pushing a piston. Its internal energy changes by:
check.why: First law: change in internal energy equals heat in minus work out, 500 minus 200 = 300 joules.

check.q: A refrigerator moves heat from its cold inside to the warm kitchen. How does this not break the second law?
choices: Refrigerators create cold rather than moving heat
The second law does not apply to machines
The kitchen is actually colder than the fridge
Electrical work is done to pump the heat, and that work becomes extra heat in the kitchen
check.why: Heat moves cold to hot only when work is supplied. The compressor does that work, and the kitchen ends up warmer overall.

check.q: Why does a bicycle pump get warm as you use it?
choices: Work done on the air raises its internal energy
Heat flows from the tire into the pump
The metal reacts chemically with air
Friction in the valve is the only cause
check.why: Compressing the gas is work done on it. By the first law, that work raises the gas's internal energy and temperature.

lessons.title: Why No Engine Is Perfect
lessons.mainIdea: A heat engine must dump some heat to a cold place, so its efficiency is limited by the temperatures it runs between.
reading: A car engine burns gasoline and turns perhaps a quarter of that chemical energy into motion. The rest leaves as hot exhaust and heat through the radiator. This is not bad engineering; it is a law of nature. Any *heat engine* takes heat from a hot source, turns some of it into work, and must dump the rest into a cold sink. If it dumped nothing, heat would be fully converted into work with no other change, and the second law forbids that.

In 1824 a young French engineer, Sadi Carnot, worked out the best any engine could possibly do. The ideal *efficiency* depends only on the temperatures of the hot source and cold sink, measured in kelvins: efficiency equals 1 minus cold temperature over hot temperature. An engine running between steam at 600 kelvin and a river at 300 kelvin could at most convert half its heat to work. Real engines, with friction and leaks, do worse. The only ways to improve are to make the hot side hotter or the cold side colder.

This is why power-plant engineers push for higher steam temperatures and why plants sit beside rivers and lakes for cooling. It is also why a car's engine needs a radiator: the cold sink has to stay cold, or the efficiency collapses. Combined-cycle gas plants reach around 60 percent by running a gas turbine and then using its hot exhaust to boil water for a second steam turbine.

Carnot was working with the old caloric theory and still got the right answer for the limit. His book sold poorly and he died of cholera at 36. Twenty-five years later, Kelvin and Clausius rebuilt his argument on Joule's finding that heat is energy, and thermodynamics became a science.

words.d: a device that takes heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work, and dumps the rest to a cold sink
useful work out divided by energy in, often written as a percent
the cooler place, like a river or the outside air, where an engine dumps its waste heat
the temperature unit that starts at absolute zero; 0 degrees Celsius is 273 kelvin

look.title: The Plant by the River
look.text: A coal-fired power station in central Illinois makes steam at about 800 kelvin and cools it with river water at about 290 kelvin. On a hot July week the river warms to 300 kelvin, and regulators also limit how warm the plant may make the river. The operators notice their output drops slightly.
look.prompt: Use Carnot's formula to explain why a warmer river lowers the plant's maximum efficiency, and why the plant cannot simply skip the cooling step.

check.q: A heat engine takes in 1000 joules of heat and does 300 joules of work. Its efficiency is:
check.why: Efficiency is work out over heat in: 300 divided by 1000 is 0.30, or 30 percent.

check.q: Which change raises the Carnot limit of an engine?
check.why: The limit is 1 minus cold over hot temperature. Raising the hot temperature makes that fraction larger.

check.q: Why must every heat engine release some heat to a cold sink?
choices: Because the second law forbids turning heat fully into work with no other change
check.why: Converting all the heat into work with nothing else changing would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

lessons.title: Entropy and the Arrow of Time
lessons.mainIdea: Entropy measures how many ways energy can be spread out, and it rises because spread-out arrangements vastly outnumber concentrated ones.
reading: Film an egg falling and breaking, then play the film backward. Everyone can tell which direction is real. Yet the laws of motion work equally well forward and backward; nothing in Newton's equations says the shards cannot leap up and reassemble. The one-way character of the world comes from the second law, and the quantity that captures it is *entropy*.

Ludwig Boltzmann, in the 1870s, gave entropy a concrete meaning. Think of the energy in a room as spread among trillions of molecules. There are only a few ways to arrange it so that all the fast molecules are in one corner and the slow ones in another. There are unimaginably many ways to arrange it so that fast and slow are mixed everywhere. Entropy counts those ways. Left alone, a system drifts toward the arrangements that are most numerous, which means the ones where energy is spread out and useless for doing work. The egg has far more ways to be broken than whole.

This is why heat flows from hot to cold, why a drop of ink spreads through water and never gathers back up, and why every engine wastes energy. Entropy can fall in one place, as when your freezer makes ice, but only by raising it more somewhere else, in the warm coils behind the freezer. Add it all up and the total always climbs. Boltzmann's equation linking entropy to the number of arrangements is carved on his gravestone in Vienna.

Living things are not exceptions. A seed grows into an ordered tree, but it does so by taking in concentrated sunlight and giving off spread-out heat. The tree's order is paid for by a larger disorder in the Sun and sky. Life rides the flow of energy downhill; it does not reverse it.

words.d: a measure of how spread out energy is, or how many microscopic arrangements match what you see
the one-way direction of change from ordered to spread-out that separates past from future
one specific arrangement of all the particles and energy in a system
happening on its own, without outside work being done

look.title: Shuffling a Deck
look.text: A new deck of cards comes sorted by suit and number. Shuffle it once and it is scrambled. Keep shuffling for an hour. The deck never returns to its sorted order, even though nothing in the rules of shuffling forbids it.
look.prompt: Why does the sorted arrangement never come back? How is a shuffled deck like heat spread evenly through a room?

check.q: Why does a drop of ink spread through a glass of water and never gather back into a drop?
choices: Ink molecules are attracted to the glass walls
There are vastly more mixed arrangements than gathered ones, so mixing is overwhelmingly likely
Water molecules push the ink outward on purpose
Gravity pulls the ink evenly in all directions
check.why: Random motion explores arrangements. Mixed arrangements outnumber the gathered one so enormously that the drop never re-forms.

check.q: A freezer turns water into orderly ice crystals. Does this break the second law?
choices: Yes, because water has no entropy
No, because more entropy is created in the warm air behind the freezer than is removed from the water
No, because ice has more entropy than water
check.why: Local entropy falls in the ice, but the freezer dumps more heat and entropy into the room. The total still rises.

check.q: Which statement about entropy and living things is accurate?
choices: Organisms build order by taking in concentrated energy and releasing spread-out heat, raising total entropy
Organisms are the only things that decrease total entropy
Growth violates the second law but only slightly
Entropy does not apply to biology
check.why: Life stays ordered by riding a flow of energy from the Sun to the cold sky. The overall entropy of Sun, Earth and space increases.

lessons.title: From Power Plant to Wall Socket
lessons.mainIdea: Most electricity comes from spinning generators driven by steam, water or wind, and the grid must balance supply and demand every second.
reading: Nearly every watt in an Illinois wall socket began as something spinning. In a coal or natural gas plant, burning fuel boils water; in a nuclear plant, splitting uranium atoms does the boiling. The steam drives a turbine, the turbine turns a *generator*, and a magnet spinning past coils of wire pushes electrons into motion. Wind turbines skip the steam and let the wind turn the generator directly. Solar panels are the odd ones out: they convert light straight to electricity with no moving parts.

Illinois is unusual. Its six nuclear plants hold eleven reactors, more than any other state, and they supply about half of the electricity generated here. The chain began in Chicago: on December 2, 1942, Enrico Fermi's team ran the first controlled nuclear chain reaction under the stands of the University of Chicago's football field, and Dresden Unit 1, near Morris, opened in 1960 as the first privately financed commercial nuclear plant in the country. Every one of these plants is still a heat engine bound by Carnot, converting roughly a third of its heat into electricity and sending the rest into cooling towers and lakes.

The *grid* is the network of high-voltage lines, transformers and substations that links plants to homes. Electricity cannot easily be stored in large amounts, so at every instant the power generated must match the power being used. Grid operators forecast demand hour by hour, ramp plants up and down, and watch frequency, which drifts if supply and demand slip apart. Transformers step voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for long-distance lines, because higher voltage means lower current and less energy lost as heat in the wires, then step it back down near your house.

Every source has trade-offs the evidence makes clear. Fossil fuels are cheap and controllable but release carbon dioxide. Nuclear plants emit almost none but produce long-lived waste. Wind and solar are clean and now inexpensive but depend on weather, which is pushing utilities toward batteries and other storage. No option is free of costs, and deciding among them is a public choice informed by, but not settled by, physics.

words.d: a machine that turns mechanical motion into electricity by moving magnets past coils of wire
a set of blades spun by steam, water or wind to drive a generator
the network of power lines, transformers and substations that carries electricity from plants to users
a device that raises or lowers the voltage of alternating current

look.title: The First Chain Reaction, Reported in Code
look.text: On December 2, 1942, after Fermi's pile under Stagg Field in Chicago went critical, physicist Arthur Compton telephoned James Conant in Washington. Accounts of the call record it in code, roughly: The Italian navigator has landed in the New World. Conant asked how the natives were, and Compton answered that they were very friendly.
look.cite: reported conversation between Arthur Compton and James Conant, December 2, 1942, as recounted in histories of the Manhattan Project
look.prompt: Why would scientists report a physics result in code, and what does the exchange tell you about how the work was viewed at the time?

check.q: In a nuclear power plant, what does the splitting of uranium atoms directly do?
choices: Produces heat that boils water into steam
Spins the turbine blades with its particles
check.why: Fission releases heat. The heat makes steam, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine drives a generator.

check.q: Why do long-distance power lines run at very high voltage?
choices: High voltage makes electrons move faster than light
Lower voltage cannot pass through transformers
At high voltage the current is lower, so less energy is lost as heat in the wires
High voltage lines are cheaper to build
check.why: Heating loss in a wire grows with the square of current. Raising voltage lets the same power flow with much less current.

check.q: Which statement about the electric grid is accurate?
choices: Electricity is stored in the wires for weeks
Supply only needs to match demand once a day
Solar panels use steam turbines like other plants
Generation must match use at every moment, or the grid frequency drifts
check.why: Large-scale storage is limited, so operators constantly balance supply and demand to keep the grid stable.

choices: a fixed amount of work always produces a fixed amount of heat
heat is a weightless fluid called caloric
water cannot be warmed by stirring
review.why: Falling weights did measurable work and the water warmed by a predictable amount every time. Heat was shown to be a form of energy.

review.q: A 2-kilogram ball moves at 4 meters per second. Its kinetic energy is:
review.why: KE = half m v squared = 0.5 times 2 times 16 = 16 joules.

review.q: Which quantity is measured in watts?
review.why: A watt is a joule per second, the unit of power, the rate of energy transfer.

review.q: A spring is compressed twice as far as before. The energy it stores is:
review.why: Elastic potential energy is half k x squared, so doubling x multiplies the energy by four.

review.q: Why does a pendulum's period stay the same when you swap a light bob for a heavy one of the same size?
choices: Gravity accelerates all masses equally, so the period depends only on length and gravity
Heavier bobs are always slower but the string compensates
Air resistance cancels the extra mass
The period depends only on how far you pull it back
review.why: Extra mass means extra gravitational force and extra inertia in the same proportion, so the motion is unchanged.

review.q: The second law of thermodynamics says that:
choices: heat never flows on its own from cold to hot
work cannot be turned into heat
review.why: Spontaneous heat flow is always from hotter to colder. Moving it the other way, as a refrigerator does, requires work.

review.q: A heat engine runs between a hot source at 500 kelvin and a cold sink at 250 kelvin. Its maximum possible efficiency is:
review.why: Carnot efficiency is 1 minus 250 over 500, which is 0.5, or 50 percent.

choices: energy is destroyed in every process
friction is unavoidable in machines only
spread-out arrangements of energy vastly outnumber concentrated ones
review.why: Random motion drives systems toward the most numerous arrangements, which are the spread-out, less useful ones.
